The 30-Point Pre-Tour Inspection

A thorough pre-tour check takes about an hour and could save your entire trip. This comprehensive 30-point checklist covers every critical system on your motorcycle. Print it out, work through it methodically, and fix anything that fails before loading up for your adventure. Read our Touring Tyre Guide: Best Tyres for UK Roads 2026 guide for more. Read our Best Bikes for the Lake District Motorcycle Touring guide for more.

Engine and Fluids

  • 1. Engine oil level — Check on a level surface with the engine warm. Top up or change if due.
  • 2. Oil condition — Dark, gritty oil needs changing. Fresh golden oil means your engine is protected.
  • 3. Coolant level — Check in the overflow reservoir when cold. Top up with the correct specification coolant.
  • 4. Brake fluid front — Should be clear amber. Dark fluid needs replacing. Level should be between min and max marks.
  • 5. Brake fluid rear — Same checks as front. Rear brakes are often neglected but equally important.
  • 6. Clutch fluid — If hydraulic, check level and condition. Low fluid can cause clutch slip or drag.

Wheels and Tyres

  • 7. Front tyre tread depth — Minimum 2mm recommended, 1mm legal minimum. Check across the full width.
  • 8. Rear tyre tread depth — Same standards. Rear tyres wear faster than fronts on most bikes.
  • 9. Tyre condition — Check for cracks, bulges, cuts, and embedded objects. Replace if any damage is found.
  • 10. Tyre pressure — Set to manufacturer's loaded touring specification when cold.
  • 11. Wheel bearings — Rock each wheel side to side. Any play means replacement needed.
  • 12. Wheel spokes — If wire wheels, check spoke tension. A loose spoke can cause wheel failure.

Brakes and Suspension

  • 13. Front brake pad thickness — Check both sides. Replace if below 2mm remaining material.
  • 14. Rear brake pad thickness — Same standard. Rear pads often wear faster with luggage weight.
  • 15. Brake disc condition — Check for scoring, warping, and minimum thickness stamps.
  • 16. Fork seals — Check for oil weeping around the fork stanchions. Leaking seals reduce damping and contaminate brake pads.
  • 17. Rear shock — Check for leaks and adjust preload for loaded touring weight.

Drive System

  • 18. Chain tension — Adjust to manufacturer specification. Usually 25-35mm of slack.
  • 19. Chain condition — Check for stiff links, excessive rust, and worn O-rings.
  • 20. Sprocket wear — Look for hooked or pointed teeth indicating replacement needed.

Electrical

  • 21. Headlight — Check main and dip beam function and alignment.
  • 22. Indicators — All four must flash at the correct rate.
  • 23. Brake light — Activated by both front lever and rear pedal.
  • 24. Horn — Must be audible. A weak horn needs replacement.
  • 25. Battery — Clean terminals, tight connections, and holds charge overnight.

Controls and Final Checks

  • 26. Throttle — Should snap shut when released. Check for fraying cables.
  • 27. Clutch — Smooth engagement with correct free play at the lever.
  • 28. Mirrors — Secure and adjustable. Replace if cracked or loose.
  • 29. Fasteners — Check critical bolts: axle nuts, brake calipers, engine mounts, subframe bolts.
  • 30. Documents — Valid MOT, insurance, driving licence, breakdown cover details packed and accessible.
If any point on this checklist raises doubt, fix it before you leave. The cost of a repair at home is always less than the cost of a breakdown on tour, both financially and in ruined riding days.
keyTakeaways: A full 30-point inspection takes around an hour and covers fluids, tyres, brakes, drive, electrics and controls.
Set tyre pressures to the manufacturer's loaded touring figure and adjust rear preload for luggage weight.
Fix anything that raises doubt before departure, as a home repair always beats a roadside breakdown.
Check documents too: valid MOT, insurance, licence and breakdown cover details packed and accessible.
Rear brake pads and tyres wear faster under luggage weight, so inspect them with two-up loading in mind.

pros: Catches faults while they are still cheap and easy to fix at home.
Builds confidence so you focus on the ride rather than the machinery.
Printable and repeatable before every trip regardless of bike type.
cons: Takes around an hour of methodical work before you can pack up.
Some checks, such as wheel bearings, need the bike off the ground.

faq.q: How long before departure should I do the checklist?
faq.a: Work through the full checklist a week or two before you leave rather than the night before. This gives time to order and fit any parts that fail inspection, and to ride the bike loaded so you can confirm everything feels right. Leave the final fluid, pressure and light checks for the morning you set off.

faq.q: What tyre pressure should I run for touring?
faq.a: Set pressures to the manufacturer's loaded or two-up specification, which is printed in the owner's manual and often on a swingarm sticker. Most bikes call for an extra 0.2 to 0.3 bar in the rear when carrying luggage or a pillion. Always check when the tyres are cold for an accurate reading.

faq.q: Do I really need to check wheel bearings?
faq.a: Yes, because bearing failure on tour causes dangerous wheel wobble and usually means recovery. Rock each wheel firmly side to side with the bike supported. Any detectable play means the bearings need replacing before you travel. It is a quick check that prevents one of the more serious roadside failures.

faq.q: What documents should I carry on a UK tour?
faq.a: Carry proof of valid insurance, your driving licence, and a note of your breakdown cover policy number and helpline. Your MOT must be current, though it is checked electronically. For trips abroad add your V5C or a VE103 hire certificate, plus any required documents for the countries you pass through.
